dialog.body: Public Works, this is Denise, how can I help you this afternoon?

Hi. My name is Marie Pucci. I'm calling about the storm drain at 701 Thames Street. That's my mother-in-law's house, down at the low corner where Thames meets Wellington. My husband Paul called on Saturday.
Okay. Saturday. Give me one second, let me pull that up. Pucci, P-U-C-C-I?
Yes.
Here it is. Paul Pucci, Saturday around two. Basement flooding, drain backup at the corner. And it says a crew would come take a look at the grate.
Right. That's what he was told. Someone would come look at it. Nobody has come to look at it. Not really.
Hm. I've actually got a note here that a crew was out at that corner this morning. Ten-forty or so.

Yeah. They pulled the leaves off the grate. That's it. My mother-in-law watched them from the front window. They were there maybe fifteen minutes. Nobody knocked, nobody looked at the pipe, nobody came to the house. The problem isn't leaves.
Okay. So what are you seeing?

During the storm Friday into Saturday that drain backed up and the whole corner was a pond. Curb to curb. You couldn't see where the sidewalk ended. And then the basement took on water. About three inches. The furnace is up on blocks, my father-in-law did that years ago, and it still got wet. The washer and dryer got wet. And this morning, after they cleared the grate, the water at the corner is still sitting there. It's not draining. Something's wrong under the street. Clearing the top doesn't fix that.
Got it. So the grate's clean, but it's still backing up underneath.
Yes. That's what I've been saying. That's what Paul said on Saturday too. The corner always does this. Every big storm it's the same corner. And every time it's somebody with a rake.
Okay. I hear you. Let me put this in properly so it doesn't just look like the first call got closed out. Bear with me one sec.
Okay.

[pause] All right. I've added that the crew cleared debris off the grate Monday morning, and that per the resident the corner is still holding water and the backup appears to be in the line under the street, not at the grate. And that you're asking for someone to look at the pipe itself.
Is someone going to come?

So, honestly, I can't book that one myself. Looking at the line underneath isn't the same crew that does the grates, and that has to go up the chain. What I can do is make sure it's flagged as an open problem with the visit noted, not a completed job. That way it doesn't fall off the list.
So nobody's coming.
Not today, no. It's in front of the right people now, though, with the details. That's better than where it was this morning.
Okay. [pause] It was supposed to be handled on Saturday. That's all I'm saying. We called, we did what we were supposed to do. And it's Monday and the corner still looks the same.
That's fair. I'm not going to argue with you on that.
Another question. Is there a claim form? For the damage. The washer, the dryer. We don't know yet about the furnace. Paul's going to look at it.

There's a claim process, yeah. That doesn't come through us, it goes through the city's claims side. I can transfer you over when we're done here, or you can call the main City Hall line and ask for claims. They'll get you the form and tell you what they need, receipts, pictures, that kind of thing.
We have pictures. Paul took a lot of pictures. Of the corner too.
Good. Hang on to all of that. Pictures of the street flooding help.
Okay. You can transfer me. [pause] Sorry. I just knocked my mug on the counter. Chipped it. That's my favorite mug. Of course.
Oh no. Today of all days.
Yeah. Fits the week. Anyway.

So before I send you over, you're all set on my end. The note's in, it's flagged that the problem's still there and that it's under the street. If anybody from Public Works calls the house, it'll be about that pipe.
I hope so. Because if it rains again like that we're going to be calling you again about the same corner.
Understood. Hold on, I'm going to connect you to claims now. If it drops, just call City Hall back and ask for them.
Okay. Thank you.
You're welcome, Marie. Hang on.
